opus-5.5.text:
Oh, that's a question very close to my heart, because games were really my first love. Before DeepMind, before neuroscience, I was designing games. I worked on Theme Park as a teenager, and then simulation games at Lionhead and my own studio, Elixir. A lot of what drew me to AI in the first place was the AI in those games. Even then, the most exciting part of a game like Theme Park was that every player's experience was a bit different, because the simulation responded to what you did.

The dream we always had back then, and couldn't quite achieve, was a truly open world: one that reacts intelligently to the player, where the characters have real motivations and memories, and where the story emerges from your choices rather than being pre-scripted. What we actually built were clever illusions. You'd have branching dialogue trees, scripted events, and a lot of smoke and mirrors to make the world feel alive. Players are very good at finding the edges of those illusions.

Over the next five to ten years, I think AI can take away a lot of those edges. A few things come together.

First, characters. With language models and agents that can plan and remember, non-player characters could hold real conversations, have goals, form opinions of you based on what you've done, and pursue their own agendas when you're not looking. That changes the texture of a world completely. It stops feeling like a theme park set and starts feeling like a living place.

Second, the world itself. We've been working on world models, systems that can generate interactive, consistent environments from a description or an image and keep them coherent as you move through them. That's still early. Consistency over long timescales and physical accuracy are hard problems. But if you extrapolate, you can imagine worlds that are generated and extended on the fly in response to where the player goes and what they're interested in. The world is effectively infinite, but still coherent.

Third, and I think this is the most interesting one, is emergent narrative. The holy grail in game design has always been a story that is genuinely yours, as dramatic and meaningful as an authored story, but shaped by your decisions. AI could act almost like a dungeon master, a director that understands pacing, tension, and what makes an experience satisfying, and adapts the world around you.

I don't think this replaces human designers. The best games will still have a strong creative vision behind them. What changes is that designers become more like architects of possibility spaces. They set the rules, tone, and themes, and the AI helps fill that space with richness no team could hand-author.

There's also a lovely loop here. Games have been incredibly useful for AI research. Atari, Go, StarCraft were all testbeds for us. Now AI might give something back to games, helping realize the kind of worlds I was imagining when I was seventeen and didn't have the technology to build. That would be a very satisfying full circle for me personally.

r001.rationale: The response discusses stories shaped by player decisions, but does not identify providing compelling content regardless of the player's choices as a central difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says AI could adapt the world and narrative around the player's choices, describing an AI director that understands pacing and tension.

r003.rationale: The response mentions world models generally, but does not propose an interactive version of Veo as a basis for generating choice-responsive game content.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I think it's a fascinating question, and it's actually quite personal for me because I started my career in games. I was writing AI for games back in the nineties, Theme Park and then Black & White, and even then the dream was always this idea of a truly living world, something that could surprise you. And the honest truth is that for the last twenty-five years, games have mostly been faking it. You have scripted behaviours, decision trees, a bit of randomness sprinkled on top, and very clever designers who hide the seams. It works, but you always eventually bump into the edges of what's been hand-authored.

What's changing now, I think, is that we're moving from authored content to generated content, and from scripted behaviour to learned behaviour. So take non-player characters first. Right now an NPC has maybe a dozen lines of dialogue and a patrol route. With the kinds of models we have today, you could have a character that actually understands the context of the world, remembers what you did three hours ago, has its own goals, and can improvise. And the interesting thing is not just that it talks fluently, it's that it can act coherently over long time horizons. That's actually a hard problem, agency over long horizons, and games are a wonderful testbed for it because the environment is rich but the stakes are low. You can fail safely.

Then the second piece is the world itself. We did some work on this with Genie, these world models that can generate an interactive, playable environment from a single image or a text prompt, and you can walk around in it and it maintains some physical consistency. Now, today that's quite limited, a few seconds, fairly low fidelity. But if you extrapolate five or ten years, I don't think it's crazy to imagine a game where the world isn't a fixed asset that shipped on a disc, but something that unfolds in response to you. You walk through a door the designer never built, and there's a room there, and it's consistent with everything you've seen. That's a very different kind of medium, actually. It's less like a film and more like a dream you can share.

I would add one caveat, which is that I don't think the designer goes away, and I'd be sad if they did. The best games have a point of view, a sense of pacing, a hand behind them. So the version I find most exciting is not the AI replacing the designer but the designer directing at a higher level of abstraction, almost like a conductor, setting the rules and the tone and the dramatic arc and letting the system fill in the texture. And actually, that's not so different from what we were trying to do in Black & White twenty years ago, we just didn't have the tools.

And then the last thing I'd say, and maybe this is the researcher in me talking, is that games are not just a consumer of this technology, they're a source of it. We trained agents in Go, in StarCraft, in Atari, and those environments taught us an enormous amount about learning, planning, and generalisation. So I suspect the relationship goes both ways. The games that come out of this will be remarkable, but the agents that learn to live inside those open worlds, to cooperate, to plan, to deal with other agents, might teach us things that matter well beyond entertainment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the limits of hand-authored content and AI-generated worlds, but does not identify providing compelling content regardless of player choices as a central difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says worlds and characters could respond to the player, but does not clearly say AI may dynamically adapt the game's narrative to the player's choices.

r003.rationale: It proposes Genie world models as a basis for generated interactive environments, but does not propose an interactive version of Veo.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most exciting possibilities is making worlds that actually respond to what you do. Open-world games already give you this tremendous sense of scale, but you eventually discover the boundaries: a character repeats their dialogue, or something you change in the world doesn’t really have consequences.

AI could help make those characters much richer. Imagine meeting someone who remembers your previous encounters, has their own goals, and reacts to how you’ve treated other people. Then a quest could emerge from that interaction, rather than having to be scripted in advance. You could get stories that feel personal because they genuinely depend on the choices you’ve made.

But there’s a difficult design problem there. Generating more content isn’t necessarily making a better game. You need coherence, pacing, and interesting constraints. If anything can happen, it can become quite unsatisfying, because you don’t understand the rules or what your decisions mean.

So over five to ten years, I’d be excited about a combination: designers creating the underlying world and its principles, and AI making what happens within it more dynamic. The test, for me, would be whether you’re surprised by something that happens, but afterwards you think, ‘Yes, that makes sense.’ That’s when a world starts to feel alive.

r001.rationale: The response describes coherence, pacing, and constraints as design challenges, but does not identify providing compelling content regardless of the player’s choices as a central difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says that within five to ten years AI could make quests and stories emerge dynamically from interactions and depend on the player’s choices.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Veo or propose a future interactive version of Veo as a basis for an open-world game.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most exciting possibilities is that the world could become much more responsive to what you actually do. Open-world games give you this wonderful sense of freedom, but at some point you discover the boundaries: a character repeats a line, or you try something the designers didn’t anticipate and the world can’t respond.

AI could help push those boundaries out. You could have characters that remember your interactions, have their own goals, and react in ways that make sense within the story. Then a quest might emerge from something you did, rather than always being something a designer placed there in advance.

But the difficult part is making that a good game. Generating endless dialogue or an enormous landscape isn’t enough. You need coherence, interesting choices, and consequences you can understand. If anything can happen arbitrarily, your decisions stop meaning very much.

So over five to ten years, I’d be excited to see designers combining carefully crafted worlds with systems that allow more improvisation inside them. You’d still have that artistic vision, but there would be much more room for the player to surprise the game—and for the game to surprise the player.

r001.rationale: The response says a good game needs coherence, interesting choices, and understandable consequences, but it does not identify compelling content regardless of the player’s choices as a central difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says quests could emerge from player actions and characters could react to them, describing narrative adapting to choices over the stated five-to-ten-year horizon.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Veo or propose an interactive version of it as a basis for an open-world game.
